Yes, there is a save-time check. It lives in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/pricing_rule/pricing_rule.py`, on the `PricingRule` class. **Call path** - `PricingRule.validate()` calls `validate_duplicate_apply_on()`. - For any `apply_on` other than "Transaction", that method looks up the child table in `apply_on_dict`. It collects the non-empty values of the matching field (`frappe.scrub(self.apply_on)`, which is `item_code` here) from each row. - It first rejects exact duplicates. If `len(values) != len(set(values))`, it throws "Duplicate Item Code found in the table". - If `apply_on == "Item Code"`, it then calls `validate_template_with_variant(values)`. **What `validate_template_with_variant(item_codes)` checks** - It runs one `frappe.get_all("Item", ...)` query with two filters at once: - `name in item_codes` - `variant_of in item_codes` - It fetches the `name` and `variant_of` fields. - An Item matches only if it is itself in the rule's list and its `variant_of` template is also in the list. That is a variant and its own template both present. - If any row matches, it takes the first one and calls `frappe.throw`. The message is "Variant {0} and its template {1} cannot both be added to the same Pricing Rule", with both names in bold. - Saving is blocked. **Scope** - The check only runs when "Apply On" is "Item Code". It is not applied to "Item Group" or "Brand". - It relies on the `variant_of` field on the Item record. It does not look at `has_variants` directly. - It only catches a variant together with the template it was created from. Two unrelated items, or two variants of the same template without the template itself, pass.

ERPNext breaks same-timestamp ties with the Stock Ledger Entry's `creation` timestamp, which is the row's insertion time. All of this is in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. I read the code but didn't run a cancellation scenario. **1. The ordering key is `(posting_datetime, creation)`.** - `posting_datetime` is built from `posting_date` and `posting_time` by `get_combine_datetime`. - The Purchase Receipt and the Material Transfer share that value, so `creation` decides which entry came first. - Every "find the neighbouring entry" query sorts by `posting_datetime` and then `creation`: - `get_stock_ledger_entries` uses `order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order}`. `get_previous_sle` calls it with `<=`, `desc` and `limit 1`. - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` uses `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1`. - `get_next_stock_reco` and `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty` use `.orderby(posting_datetime).orderby(creation)`. **2. "Previous" entry selection.** - `get_stock_ledger_entries` always filters `is_cancelled = 0`, so a cancelled entry is never picked as the previous one. - When `operator` is `<=` or `>` and a `name` is given, it adds `name != %(name)s`. The current SLE can't match itself on an equal timestamp. - In `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`, when the args carry `creation` and `sle_id` and the entry isn't cancelled, the operator becomes `<=` and it adds `creation < '<creation>'`. That keeps only equal-timestamp entries created before the current one. When `exclude_current_voucher=True` it uses `voucher_no != current` instead. Stock Reconciliation uses this path through `get_stock_reco_qty_shift`. **3. "Future / current" entry selection in `update_qty_in_future_sle`.** - The base filter is `posting_datetime > current`. - If the entry has `creation` and isn't being cancelled, it adds `OR (posting_datetime == current AND creation > current.creation)`. Only same-second entries created later count as "future". - On cancellation (`is_cancelled` is true) that tie-break is dropped, so only strictly later timestamps are shifted. The cancelled row is excluded by `is_cancelled == 0`. - `get_next_reco_datetime_condition` mirrors this. On cancel it uses `posting_datetime >= current`. Otherwise it uses `> current` or `== current AND creation > creation`. - `get_datetime_limit_condition` bounds the update range with `posting_datetime < reco_dt OR (== AND creation < reco.creation)`. **4. Negative-stock validation.** - `update_qty_in_future_sle` ends by calling `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle`. - That function returns early if negative stock is allowed. It also returns early for incoming entries (`actual_qty >= 0`) unless the voucher is a Stock Reconciliation. - Otherwise `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty` looks for the first non-cancelled SLE of the same item and warehouse, from another voucher, at or after the cancelled entry's `posting_datetime`, whose recalculated `qty_after_transaction < 0`. It sorts by `posting_datetime` and then `creation`. - If it finds one, `is_negative_with_precision` rounds the deficit to the system float precision and ignores anything under 0.0001. Then it raises `NegativeStockError` with the "units needed ... to complete this transaction" message. - Batch quantities get the same check in `get_future_sle_with_negative_batch_qty`. It uses a running window sum `over (order by posting_datetime, creation)`. **Net effect.** If the Purchase Receipt is cancelled, the Material Transfer's outgoing entry at the same second is treated as following the removed receipt. Its recalculated balance goes negative and the check blocks the cancellation. If the transfer is cancelled instead, the receipt can't be mistaken for a "future" entry. Ordering is deterministic and doesn't depend on which entry the database happens to return first. I didn't open the repost path (`update_entries_after`). It uses the same `creation`-based conditions, for example around lines 1654 and 2163 of the same file.

ERPNext breaks same-timestamp ties with the `creation` timestamp of each Stock Ledger Entry (SLE). It does this in three places, and `cancelled=True` switches the tie-break off in two of them. I read the code but did not run it. **1. Order of entries** - Entries are ordered by `posting_datetime`, which is `posting_date` and `posting_time` combined by `get_combine_datetime` in `erpnext/stock/utils.py`. - Entries with the same `posting_datetime` are then ordered by `creation`. - The ordering `posting_datetime`, then `creation` appears in: - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` (`ORDER BY posting_datetime DESC, creation DESC LIMIT 1`) - `get_sle_against_current_voucher` - `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty` - `get_future_stock_vouchers` in `erpnext/accounts/utils.py` **2. Entry point for a cancel** - `repost_current_voucher` in `stock_ledger.py` passes `posting_date`, `posting_time`, `voucher_no`, `sle_id` (the SLE name), `creation` and `cancelled` to `update_entries_after`. - It then calls `update_qty_in_future_sle(args, allow_negative_stock)`. **3. Choosing the "previous" entry** (`get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`) - Normally it takes the latest non-cancelled SLE with `posting_datetime < current`. - If `creation` and `sle_id` are set and the call is not a cancellation, the operator becomes `<=` and the filter `creation < '<this SLE's creation>'` is added. An earlier-created entry at the same second therefore counts as "previous", and the current entry and later-created ones do not. - With `exclude_current_voucher=True`, which Stock Reconciliation uses, it filters on `voucher_no != current` instead. - All of these queries use `is_cancelled = 0`, so a cancelled SLE never counts as previous. **4. Choosing the "current" entries** (`get_sle_against_current_voucher`, used by `process_sle_against_current_timestamp`) - It selects non-cancelled SLEs for the same item and warehouse at exactly the same `posting_datetime`, ordered by `creation` ascending, with `FOR UPDATE`. - For a normal submit it adds `creation == kwargs.creation`, so only that SLE is picked. - When `cancelled=True` it drops that filter. Every non-cancelled entry at that second is then reprocessed in `creation` order. - This is what stops a surviving same-second entry (say the Material Transfer after a cancelled Purchase Receipt) from keeping stale balances. **5. Shifting future balances and checking for negative stock** (`update_qty_in_future_sle`) - The "future" set is `posting_datetime > current`. - For a non-cancelled entry with a `creation` value, it also includes `posting_datetime == current AND creation > current creation`. - For a cancelled entry (`is_cancelled` set), the `creation` clause is skipped. Every non-cancelled entry at that timestamp then receives the reversed qty shift, because the cancelled row itself is already excluded by `is_cancelled = 0`. - It then calls `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle`. That calls `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty`, which looks for the first SLE with `posting_datetime >= current`, `voucher_no != this voucher`, `is_cancelled = 0` and `qty_after_transaction < 0`, ordered by `posting_datetime` then `creation`. - Because the order is deterministic, the negative balance reported is the first real one in `creation` order. The check is skipped when `allow_negative_stock` is set or the item allows negative stock. - There is a test for this: `test_update_qty_in_future_sle_shifts_same_timestamp_later_entry`. **6. The reposting loop** - `repost_future_sle` runs `update_entries_after` per item and warehouse. It passes `creation` along, so the repost starts from the correct position within the same second. - `get_future_stock_vouchers` returns the affected vouchers ordered by `Min(posting_datetime)`, then `Min(creation)`.

final answer
Ordering is not decided by the timestamp alone. ERPNext breaks ties on the same `posting_datetime` using the SLE's `creation` timestamp. When a transaction is cancelled, it uses the `is_cancelled` / `cancelled` flags to switch the comparison. All the code below is in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. **1. The sort key is `(posting_datetime, creation)`.** - `posting_datetime` is the combined posting date and time, built with `get_combine_datetime`. - `get_stock_ledger_entries` filters `is_cancelled = 0` and sorts with `order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order}`. - `get_previous_sle` calls it with `"<=", "desc", limit 1`. If a reference SLE name is passed, it adds `name != %(name)s` so the entry doesn't return itself. - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` uses the same ordering (`posting_datetime desc, creation desc limit 1 for update`), but it filters on the combined datetime. - Because `creation` is part of the order, two SLEs with identical posting date and time still have a deterministic order. **2. Picking the "previous" SLE for a voucher in `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`.** - Normal case: it takes entries with `posting_datetime < current`. - If the args carry both `creation` and `sle_id`, and `cancelled` is false, it switches the operator to `<=`. It also adds `creation < '<this sle's creation>'`. This is the exact-timestamp tie-break. Entries at the same second count as "previous" only if they were created before this SLE. - In the cancelled case, that branch is skipped. The cancelled SLEs are already `is_cancelled = 1` and excluded. The plain `<` comparison then gives the previous entry before the timestamp. - `repost_current_voucher` passes `sle_id`, `creation` and `cancelled` into `update_entries_after`, which calls this function. - Calls with `exclude_current_voucher=True` (used by `get_stock_reco_qty_shift`) skip the creation clause and use `voucher_no != current`. **3. Selecting "future" SLEs in `update_qty_in_future_sle`.** - The base condition is `posting_datetime > current`. - If `creation` is present and the entry is not cancelled, it adds `OR (posting_datetime == current AND creation > this.creation)`. Same-second entries created later are therefore treated as future. - On cancellation (`is_cancelled` true), that clause is dropped and the cancelled voucher's quantity is reversed across the future entries. - Same-second entries, which may be ordered either side, are handled by the later negative-stock check below. That check uses `>=` on the timestamp and excludes only the current voucher, so a same-second entry can't escape the check. - The same pattern appears in the next-reconciliation helpers: - `get_next_reco_datetime_condition` uses `posting_datetime >= current` when cancelled. Otherwise it uses `>` current, or `==` current with `creation >` this SLE's creation. - `get_datetime_limit_condition` uses `< datetime`, or `==` with `creation <` the reconciliation's creation. **4. Negative-stock validation.** - After shifting future balances, `update_qty_in_future_sle` calls `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle`. - That calls `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty`. It looks for the first non-cancelled SLE for the same item and warehouse with `voucher_no != this voucher`, `posting_datetime >= this datetime`, and `qty_after_transaction < 0`. It orders by `posting_datetime, creation`. - It uses `>=` rather than `>`, so entries at the same second are included even though their relative order is only fixed by `creation`. - If the deficit survives `is_negative_with_precision`, it raises `NegativeStockError` ("units needed … to complete this transaction"). The batch version, `get_future_sle_with_negative_batch_qty`, works the same way. I read this from the code and did not run any scenario, so the Purchase Receipt and Material Transfer example is inferred from the queries.

Same-timestamp ties are broken by each Stock Ledger Entry's `creation` timestamp. When a transaction is cancelled, the code looks at the whole timestamp bucket instead of one entry. I read the code and did not run it. **1. A combined datetime plus `creation` as the sort key** - Every query builds `posting_datetime` from `posting_date` and `posting_time` with `get_combine_datetime`. It then sorts by `posting_datetime`, then `creation`. - This applies in `get_stock_ledger_entries` (`order by posting_datetime {order}, creation {order}`, with `is_cancelled = 0`) and in `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`. It also applies in `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty`, `get_sle_against_current_voucher`, and `get_balance_qty_from_sle` in `stock_balance.py`. - The Purchase Receipt and the Material Transfer therefore get a stable order from which entry was created first. Cancelled rows are filtered out of every one of these queries. **2. How "previous" is chosen** - The reposting class is `update_entries_after`, in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. Its `initialize_previous_data` calls `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher(args)`. - When the entry is not being cancelled (`sle_id` and `creation` are set, `cancelled` is false), the function changes its filter. It switches the operator to `<=` and adds `creation < '<this sle's creation>'`. - The "previous" row is then either strictly earlier in time, or at the same timestamp and created earlier. It cannot be a same-second entry that was created later. **3. The cancel path** - `repost_current_voucher` passes `cancelled=cancelled` and `sle_id` into `update_entries_after`. - In `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher`, the `creation <` condition is skipped when `cancelled` is true. The default operator is `<`, so the previous entry is the last non-cancelled entry strictly before that timestamp. - The cancelled voucher's own entries are marked `is_cancelled = 1`, so they never show up as "previous". - `get_sle_against_current_voucher` normally filters on `creation == kwargs.creation`, which picks out the current entry. When `cancelled` is set, it drops that filter. It then returns every non-cancelled entry at that exact `posting_datetime` for the item and warehouse, ordered by `creation` ascending. `process_sle_against_current_timestamp` replays all of them in order. - So, for example, a same-second Material Transfer is replayed in its creation order after the Purchase Receipt is cancelled. It is not matched by a fragile single-row lookup. **4. Future entries** - `get_future_entries_to_fix` calls `get_sle_after_datetime`. That uses `get_stock_ledger_entries(args, ">", "asc", for_update=True)`, starting from the previous SLE. The `>` operator and the `name != %(name)s` condition keep the current row from being counted twice. **5. Where negative stock is validated** - During replay, `validate_negative_stock(sle)` checks `qty_after_transaction + actual_qty - reserved_stock`. It runs on the replayed running balance, so it sees entries in the deterministic order above. - The separate check `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle` calls `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty`. That looks at non-cancelled entries from the same item and warehouse at or after the timestamp (`posting_datetime >=`), excluding the current `voucher_no`. It sorts by `posting_datetime` then `creation`, and takes the first row with `qty_after_transaction < 0`. - `get_datetime_limit_condition` (`sle.posting_datetime == dt and sle.creation < detail.creation`) uses the same rule for other lookups. **6. Where it is triggered** - `repost_future_sle` (via `RepostItemValuation.repost`) loops over `items_to_be_repost`. For each item and warehouse it builds `update_entries_after({... "creation": ..., ...})`. Each repost starts at that timestamp and `creation`.

When a transaction is cancelled, the code changes which of the two keys it uses for the "previous" and "future" lookups. I read the code in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. I didn't run it, and I didn't trace every caller. **1. Ordering key.** Every ledger query orders by `posting_datetime` and then `creation`. `posting_date` and `posting_time` are combined into one `posting_datetime` by `get_combine_datetime`, in `erpnext/stock/utils.py`. Same-second entries are then separated by `creation`. **2. Entry point.** `repost_current_voucher` passes `creation`, the SLE name (`sle_id`) and a `cancelled` flag into `update_entries_after`. It then calls `update_qty_in_future_sle`. **3. Selecting the "previous" SLE.** - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher` filters on `is_cancelled = 0` and orders by `posting_datetime desc, creation desc` with `limit 1`. - On a normal post, when `creation` and `sle_id` are present and `cancelled` is false, it switches the operator to `<=` and adds `creation < '<this creation>'`. The previous entry is then the latest one at the same timestamp that was created before this one. The Purchase Receipt therefore sorts before the Material Transfer that was created after it. - On cancel, that `creation` condition is skipped. The cancelled SLE already has `is_cancelled = 1`, so it is excluded by the `is_cancelled = 0` filter. The previous entry is simply the last live entry before the timestamp. - `get_stock_ledger_entries` (used by `get_previous_sle`, `get_sle_after_datetime` and `get_future_entries_to_repost`) uses the same `posting_datetime`, then `creation` ordering. It adds `name != <sle name>` when the operator is `>` or `<=`, so the entry never compares against itself. - Batch and non-batch valuation (`deprecated_serial_batch.py`, `get_last_sle_for_non_batch`) uses the same rule: `posting_datetime < X OR (posting_datetime == X AND creation < this.creation)`. **4. Selecting the "current" SLE.** `get_sle_against_current_voucher` matches the same item, warehouse and `posting_datetime`, with `is_cancelled = 0`, ordered by `creation asc`. It adds `creation == kwargs.creation` only when not cancelled. On cancel it returns all live entries at that second, in creation order, so reposting walks them in a deterministic order. **5. Shifting future balances.** `update_qty_in_future_sle` builds its future condition as `posting_datetime > X`. When `creation` is present and the SLE is not cancelled, it also includes `posting_datetime == X AND creation > this.creation`. - A normal post therefore also shifts later-created entries at the same second. - A cancel only shifts strictly later timestamps. It deliberately skips the same-second rows, because their balances are handled by the full repost with the cancelled entry excluded. - `get_datetime_limit_condition` bounds the update at the next Stock Reconciliation using the same `(datetime, creation)` tuple comparison. **6. Negative-stock validation.** `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle` then calls `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty`. It looks for any live SLE (`is_cancelled = 0`, `qty_after_transaction < 0`) for the item and warehouse with a different `voucher_no`. The entry must have `posting_datetime >= X`, and results are ordered by `posting_datetime, creation`. - It uses `>=`, so same-second entries are included in the check. - It excludes the voucher's own entries. - It ignores cancelled rows. Cancelling the Purchase Receipt therefore cannot be masked by the cancelled row, and a Material Transfer left negative by the cancel is caught. - The deterministic `creation` ordering decides which offending SLE is reported first. A separate path, `update_entries_after.validate_negative_stock`, runs during reposting and works on the same ordered data.

ERPNext breaks same-timestamp ties with the Stock Ledger Entry `creation` timestamp. It also skips cancelled entries and special-cases the entry being cancelled. All of this is in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. I read the code but did not run it or the tests. **1. Ordering key** - Every SLE has `posting_datetime`, built from the date and time by `get_combine_datetime` in `erpnext/stock/utils.py`. - When two entries have the same `posting_datetime`, the order is decided by `creation`, the row's insertion time. The Purchase Receipt and Material Transfer in your example are ordered this way. - Every query that decides "before" or "after" sorts by `posting_datetime`, then `creation`, and ignores `is_cancelled = 1` rows. **2. Choosing the previous entry** - `get_previous_sle_of_current_voucher(args, operator="<", exclude_current_voucher=False)` picks the previous entry. - Its query filters on the item and warehouse, `is_cancelled = 0` and `posting_datetime < …`. It sorts by `posting_datetime DESC, creation DESC`, takes `LIMIT 1`, and uses `FOR UPDATE`. - For a live entry (it has `creation` and `sle_id`, and `cancelled` is not set), it changes the operator to `<=` and adds `creation < <this creation>`. That picks up earlier entries at the identical timestamp and excludes this entry and later ones. - For a cancelled entry, that branch is skipped. The strict `<` on `posting_datetime` is used, and `is_cancelled = 0` removes the cancelled row itself. - `update_entries_after.repost_stock_ledgers` and `initialize_previous_data` call this function. Reposting starts from that previous entry's `qty_after_transaction` and valuation. - The deprecated serial/batch code applies the same rule. In `get_last_sle_for_non_batch` it uses `posting_datetime < X` OR (`posting_datetime == X` AND `creation < sle.creation`). If there is no `creation`, it adds 1 ms to the timestamp. **3. Choosing the current voucher's entries** - `get_sle_against_current_voucher` matches `posting_datetime ==` the timestamp for the same item and warehouse, with `is_cancelled = 0`. It orders by `creation ASC` and uses `FOR UPDATE`. - For a normal post it also requires `creation == kwargs.creation`, so only that exact row is picked. - For a cancellation (`kwargs.cancelled` set), it returns all same-timestamp entries in creation order. **4. Shifting later balances and validating negative stock** - `update_qty_in_future_sle(args, allow_negative_stock)` adds the cancelled entry's `actual_qty` (or the reconciliation shift) to later entries' `qty_after_transaction`. - Its "future" condition is `posting_datetime > T`. Only for a non-cancelled entry does it add `(posting_datetime == T AND creation > args.creation)`. - For a cancellation, `is_cancelled` is set, so that clause is dropped. Every live entry after the cancelled one is then shifted, whatever its `creation` value. The cancelled row's own `creation` can't be used to split the equal-timestamp group. - The shift stops at the next Stock Reconciliation. `get_next_stock_reco` finds it, ordered by `posting_datetime, creation`. `get_next_reco_datetime_condition` and `get_datetime_limit_condition` use `posting_datetime < T OR (== T AND creation < reco.creation)`. - The function then calls `validate_negative_qty_in_future_sle`. That calls `get_future_sle_with_negative_qty`, which looks for the first live entry from `posting_datetime >=` T (excluding the same `voucher_no`) with `qty_after_transaction < 0`, ordered by `posting_datetime, creation`. - If the first such entry is negative beyond the precision tolerance, it raises `NegativeStockError`. `is_negative_with_precision` does the tolerance check. - Because the equal-timestamp group is ordered by `creation`, a negative balance caused by the cancellation is found at a definite position and reported against a definite voucher. **5. Reposting loop** - `repost_stock_ledgers` works through future entries from `_get_future_entries_to_repost` and skips ones it has already done. It records the earliest datetime per item and warehouse and seeds `prev_sle_dict` using the function in section 2. - `validate_previous_sle_qty` then warns only if the previous entry's balance is negative and the new entry is incoming. The test `test_update_qty_in_future_sle_shifts_same_timestamp_later_entry` in `test_stock_ledger_entry.py` covers the same-timestamp shift.

The incoming rate comes from a value stored on the source Delivery Note Item. It is not recomputed when the Purchase Receipt is made. **Where this happens:** `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. I read this code but didn't run it. **How it works:** 1. When the Purchase Receipt's stock ledger entry is processed, the code checks `is_internal_transfer(sle)`. That check is true when the receipt's `is_internal_supplier` is set and its `represents_company` equals its `company`. It applies to Purchase Receipt and Purchase Invoice entries that have a `voucher_detail_no`. 2. If so, it calls `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer(sle)`. The docstring says that for an inter-company transfer, the incoming rate is the average of the outgoing rate. 3. That function follows the Purchase Receipt Item's `delivery_note_item` link back to the Delivery Note Item. For a Purchase Invoice it uses `sales_invoice_item` and the Sales Invoice Item instead. 4. It reads the `incoming_rate` field from that source row. 5. It adds any landed cost: `landed_cost_voucher_amount / abs(actual_qty)` from the receipt's own item row. 6. The result, `rate + lcv_rate`, is used as the receipt's incoming rate. The code path at about line 1040 has a comment saying this anchors the entry to the Delivery Note or Sales Invoice `incoming_rate`. It avoids a stale Purchase Receipt `valuation_rate` leaking into COGS. **Fixed or fresh:** - The base rate is the `incoming_rate` saved on the Delivery Note Item. That is the outgoing valuation of the source warehouse stock, set when the Delivery Note was made. Nothing at receipt time recalculates it from the destination warehouse's stock or the receipt's own `valuation_rate`. - The one value computed at receipt time is the landed cost voucher amount, which is added on top of the fixed rate.

The Purchase Receipt uses the Delivery Note's stored rate, not a fresh one. That rate was fixed when the Delivery Note was submitted. The only part computed at receipt time is the landed cost voucher amount, which is added on top. **Where the rate is set on the receipt: `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate` in `erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py`** - It only runs for a Purchase Receipt, or a Purchase Invoice with `update_stock`. It skips returns and skips anything that isn't an internal transfer (`is_internal_transfer()`). - It calls `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer`. For each item that is linked to a Delivery Note Item, this reads `incoming_rate` from that Delivery Note Item when the supplier is internal (`is_internal_supplier`). Otherwise it reads the Delivery Note Item's `rate`. The value is multiplied by the conversion factor and saved as `sales_incoming_rate` on the receipt item. - If an item has no Delivery Note link, it computes a rate fresh with `get_incoming_rate`. That call uses `from_warehouse`, the posting date and time, and a negative quantity. This is the only fresh calculation in the flow. - Unless the Stock Settings option `allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` is on, `set_incoming_rate` overwrites each item's `rate` with `sales_incoming_rate`. It also zeroes the discount and margin fields. **Where the stock ledger gets its rate: `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer` in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`** - `update_entries_after.get_incoming_outgoing_rate_from_transaction` calls it for Purchase Receipt and Purchase Invoice entries that are internal transfers. - It looks up the linked `delivery_note_item` (or `sales_invoice_item`) and reads that item's stored `incoming_rate`. This is the valuation rate recorded when the Delivery Note was submitted. - It then adds `landed_cost_voucher_amount / abs(actual_qty)` from the receipt item. - This is the rate the ledger uses when it reposts entries. The test `test_internal_transfer_pr_incoming_sle_anchored_to_dn_rate` checks that a wrong `valuation_rate` on the receipt item is corrected back to the Delivery Note's `incoming_rate` (100).

**Short answer:** the Purchase Receipt (PR) does not compute a fresh rate. It reuses the `incoming_rate` stored on the source Delivery Note Item (DN Item). That value was fixed when the Delivery Note (DN) was posted. The only thing added at receipt time is any landed cost. **How it works** - The logic is in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`. In the stock ledger's per-entry processing (around lines 1032–1044), a Purchase Receipt or Purchase Invoice line gets this treatment when it has a `voucher_detail_no` and `is_internal_transfer(sle)` is true. - `is_internal_transfer` is true when the document has `is_internal_supplier` set and `represents_company` equals `company`. - For those lines the code calls `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer(sle)` (around line 2540). - That function follows the PR Item's `delivery_note_item` link to the Delivery Note Item and reads its `incoming_rate`. For a Purchase Invoice, it uses the `sales_invoice_item` link to the Sales Invoice Item instead. - It then adds `landed_cost_voucher_amount / abs(actual_qty)` from the PR Item, so landed cost vouchers do change the final rate. - The result is applied as follows: - Inward entry (`actual_qty > 0`): it overrides `sle.incoming_rate`, but only if the rate is non-zero. - Outward entry (`actual_qty < 0`): it overrides `sle.outgoing_rate`. - The inline comment explains why. Without this, the inward entry could inherit a stale PR valuation rate, and the gap would leak into COGS through divisional loss. A test in `test_purchase_receipt.py` (around line 1913) checks that the internal-transfer PR's inward entry uses `DN.incoming_rate`. **Where the DN's `incoming_rate` comes from:** it is the valuation (outgoing) rate of the source warehouse when the DN was submitted, so it is already fixed on the DN Item by the time the PR is made. I did not trace the code that writes it onto the DN Item. **Caveat:** I only read the override at lines 1032–1044. Line 1472 also calls `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer`, and I did not check that call.

I've traced the code and I'm ready to answer. **The Purchase Receipt (PR) uses the incoming rate stored on the source Delivery Note (DN) item. It does not compute a fresh valuation at receipt time.** There is one exception, a PR line with no DN link, covered below. A landed cost voucher amount is added on top at ledger-posting time. **1. Document validation: `BuyingController.set_incoming_rate`** (`erpnext/controllers/buying_controller.py:606`) - It runs from `AccountsController.validate`, right after `InternalTransferService(self).validate()`. - It applies only to a PR, or to a Purchase Invoice with `update_stock`. It skips returns and anything that isn't an internal transfer. - It calls `set_sales_incoming_rate_for_internal_transfer` (line 647), which sets `d.sales_incoming_rate` on each item: - **PR line linked to a DN item (the normal case):** it reads `incoming_rate` from that `Delivery Note Item` with `frappe.db.get_value`, multiplied by the conversion factor. For a Purchase Invoice linked to a Sales Invoice (SI) item it reads `rate`, unless the supplier is internal, in which case it reads `incoming_rate`. The DN's stored value is reused. - **PR line with no DN link:** it computes a rate with `get_incoming_rate(...)`. This uses the `from_warehouse`, the PR's posting date and time, and the negative stock quantity. `InternalTransferService.validate_reference` makes the link mandatory in the normal flow, so this branch is a fallback. - Unless Stock Settings `allow_internal_transfer_at_arms_length_price` is set, it zeroes the discount and margin on each row and overwrites `d.rate` with `sales_incoming_rate`. It then shows the message "Item rate has been updated as per valuation rate since its an internal stock transfer." **2. Stock ledger posting: `get_incoming_rate_for_inter_company_transfer(sle)`** (`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py:2540`) - It is called from two places in `stock_ledger.py`: around line 1040 when the stock ledger entry (SLE) is built, and around line 1472 when the incoming rate is computed. Both are guarded by `is_internal_transfer(sle)`, which checks `is_internal_supplier` and `represents_company == company`. - It follows `voucher_detail_no` on the PR Item to its `delivery_note_item` (a Sales Invoice Item for a Purchase Invoice). It then reads `incoming_rate` from that `Delivery Note Item` with `get_cached_value`. - It adds `landed_cost_voucher_amount / abs(actual_qty)` from the PR item. That is the one part that can change after the DN. - The result becomes the SLE's `incoming_rate`. For outgoing rows it becomes `outgoing_rate`. - A code comment in the same file says this anchors the PR to the DN rate. Without it, a stale PR `valuation_rate` would leak the gap into COGS. **Where the DN's `incoming_rate` comes from:** it is set by `SellingController.set_incoming_rate` (`selling_controller.py:515`). That is the outgoing valuation rate when the DN is validated or submitted. So the PR inherits that fixed rate. final answer
**Short answer:** With Update Stock off, the invoice posts only one expense-side debit per item. With Update Stock on, it can also post a Purchase Price Variance debit. All of this is in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`, in `make_item_gl_entries` and `make_stock_adjustment_entry`. **Update Stock off (the `else` branch of `make_item_gl_entries`)** - The invoice posts a single debit to `item.expense_account` for the full billed amount, `base_amount` from `TaxService.get_amount_and_base_amount`. The supplier (payable) account is credited as usual. - For an item linked to a Purchase Receipt, `item.expense_account` is normally Stock Received But Not Billed (SRBNB). The debit therefore clears the SRBNB that the receipt booked. - The Purchase Receipt already booked the stock at standard cost and the Purchase Price Variance (PPV). The code comment says booking PPV again here would double count it and leave SRBNB partly uncleared. - This path writes no stock ledger entry and no Stock-in-Hand entry. It also never calls `make_stock_adjustment_entry`, so no PPV line is written. - Two optional extras can appear: - A reversal of the provisional-expense entry, if provisional accounting is on. - An exchange-rate discrepancy pair, debiting the expense account and crediting the exchange gain/loss account. This applies only when the PR's exchange rate differs from the invoice's, `adjust_incoming_rate` is off, and the line is linked to a PR. **Update Stock on (the first branch, when `auto_accounting_for_stock` is also on and the item is a stock item or fixed asset)** - `make_stock_adjustment_entry` works out `warehouse_debit_amount` as `valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor`. Here `valuation_rate` is the rate the invoice itself used for the stock entry. - It compares that figure with the stock value difference from the Stock Ledger Entries (SLEs) the invoice itself created. - If they differ, it posts a debit of `warehouse_debit_amount − stock_amount` to the variance account. - For Standard Cost items, `get_stock_variance_account` returns the PPV account from `get_purchase_price_variance_account`. - For other items it returns the company's default expense account. - The same function handles returns, where `stock_amount` is compared against the SLE value. - The `item.expense_account` debit is then posted for the `warehouse_debit_amount` returned from `make_stock_adjustment_entry`. This is the stock value actually booked, not the billed amount. - The debit lands on `expense_account`, which in practice is the Stock-in-Hand/inventory account. - Landed-cost credits, sub-contracting raw-material credits and the `from_warehouse` transfer entries can also appear on this path. **Difference** - **Update Stock off:** the invoice only clears SRBNB at the billed amount. The standard-cost versus actual-price difference stays as PPV in the Purchase Receipt's GL entries. - **Update Stock on:** the invoice itself moves stock, so it books the stock value and any PPV (standard-cost items) or default-expense variance (other items) between the billed valuation and the SLE value. I didn't read the Purchase Receipt code that books PPV, so the claim that the receipt books it rests on the code comment in the invoice path.

final answer
**Update Stock off** The invoice posts no Purchase Price Variance (PPV) and no stock adjustment. The item's expense side is one debit to the item's expense account for the full billed amount, with the supplier credited by the same amount. - The code is `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries` in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`, in the `else:` branch around lines 319–350. - The branch is taken because `doc.update_stock` is false, so the `update_stock and auto_accounting_for_stock` stock branch is skipped. - The debit is `base_amount`, with `against` set to the supplier. It uses `item.expense_account`, or the deferred expense account if deferred expense is enabled and the invoice isn't a return. - With a Purchase Receipt and perpetual inventory, that expense account is normally the "Stock Received But Not Billed" (SRBNB) account. The debit therefore clears the SRBNB the receipt booked. - A code comment in that branch says the receipt already booked the stock at standard cost and the PPV. Booking PPV again here would double count it and leave SRBNB partly uncleared. - The only other expense-side entry is the exchange-rate discrepancy pair. It applies when the conversion rate differs from the receipt's: a debit to the expense account and a credit to the exchange gain/loss account. **Update Stock on** When `update_stock` and `auto_accounting_for_stock` are both on and the item is a stock item, the invoice does its own stock posting. - `make_stock_adjustment_entry` (line 535) computes `warehouse_debit_amount` as `valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor`. - It compares that with the actual stock value difference from the invoice's own Stock Ledger Entries. - If the two differ, it posts an extra "Stock Adjustment" debit. For a Standard Cost item, `get_stock_variance_account` sends that debit to the Purchase Price Variance account from `get_purchase_price_variance_account`. For other items it goes to the company's default expense account. - That adjustment is not posted for a return that has a `return_against` (the first branch at line 545 needs no `return_against` or an internal supplier). - The item's expense account is then debited with the adjusted `warehouse_debit_amount`. This is the stock-value amount, not the billed amount. - If the item has a `from_warehouse`, the debit goes to that warehouse's inventory account instead, as shown in lines 190–248. - Landed-cost entries and subcontracting raw-material credits are also posted in this branch. **Difference** With Update Stock off, the item's expense account is debited the full billed amount. The standard-versus-purchase-price difference stays in the Purchase Receipt's PPV entry, posted via `get_divisional_loss_account` in the receipt's `gl_composer.py`. With Update Stock on, the invoice posts its own stock movement and its own PPV debit.

final answer
**With Update Stock off, the invoice posts one expense-side debit and no Purchase Price Variance (PPV) entry. With Update Stock on, it can also post a PPV debit.** The code is in `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer`, in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`. I traced it by reading the code and did not run it. **Update Stock off** - The item goes through the `else` branch of the item loop, because the `doc.update_stock and doc.auto_accounting_for_stock and item in stock_items` test fails. - That branch posts a single debit to `item.expense_account`, for the full billed amount (`base_amount` from `tax_service.get_amount_and_base_amount`). The matching credit is the supplier payable. For a stock item linked to a Purchase Receipt, that expense account is Stock Received But Not Billed (SRBNB), so the debit clears the receipt's SRBNB credit. - The code comment at about lines 331–336 says why there is no PPV entry. The Purchase Receipt already booked the stock at standard cost and the PPV. Booking PPV again here would double count it and leave SRBNB partly uncleared. - The PPV in question is the gap between the receipt rate and the standard cost. The Purchase Receipt composer (`PurchaseReceiptGLComposer`, in `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py`) books it to the account returned by `get_purchase_price_variance_account`. - There is one optional extra pair. If the exchange rate differs from the receipt's and the invoice isn't adjusting the incoming rate, it posts an expense debit and an exchange gain/loss credit. **Update Stock on** - The item goes through the first branch. `make_stock_adjustment_entry` computes `warehouse_debit_amount` as `valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor`. - It then debits `item.expense_account` for that warehouse amount. This is the `else` path under `from_warehouse`, so it applies when the item has no source warehouse. The stock ledger entries create the matching inventory-account debit, so the stock lines up with what is actually received into the warehouse. - If the stock value from the stock ledger entry differs from that amount, `make_stock_adjustment_entry` adds a "Stock Adjustment" debit, with the item's expense account as the `against` account. The account comes from `get_stock_variance_account`. - For a Standard Cost item, `get_stock_variance_account` returns `get_purchase_price_variance_account(item_code, company)`, so the difference lands in the PPV account. Other items use the company's `default_expense_account`. - The same function handles returns with Update Stock on, where it posts the difference against the stock value the original receipt booked. - When the item has a `from_warehouse`, the composer also posts an inventory-account debit and a negative-debit entry on the source warehouse account. - Landed-cost and subcontracting supplier-warehouse credits can also appear in this branch.

final answer
**Short answer:** With Update Stock off, the invoice posts one expense-side debit per item and no Purchase Price Variance (PPV) entry. With Update Stock on, it also posts a stock-adjustment line that goes to the PPV account. All the code below is in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`. **Update Stock off** The stock branch is skipped, and the item goes through the `else` branch of the per-item loop (about lines 319–350). That branch posts: - **Debit:** `item.expense_account` for the full billed amount (`base_amount`). For a stock item linked to a Purchase Receipt (PR), this account is the Stock Received But Not Billed (SRBNB) account. The `against` field is the supplier, and `cost_center` and `project` are set on the line. - **Credit:** the supplier payable, posted by the party/payable part of the invoice's GL code. - **Taxes:** posted separately by `make_tax_gl_entries`. No inventory account or PPV entry is posted. The code comment at lines 331–336 says the PR already booked the stock at the standard rate and the PPV. Booking PPV again would double count it and leave SRBNB partly uncleared. So the invoice only clears SRBNB at the full billed amount against the supplier. The only other expense-side line is an exchange-rate difference. If the PR and invoice conversion rates differ, a debit to the expense account and a credit to `exchange_gain_loss_account` are posted. **Update Stock on** When `doc.update_stock` and `auto_accounting_for_stock` are set for a stock item, the first branch (about lines 180–270) runs and calls `make_stock_adjustment_entry`. This posts: - **Debit:** `item.expense_account` for the warehouse amount (`warehouse_debit_amount`), computed from the stock-ledger value (`valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor`, or the voucher's stock value difference). - **Debit or credit:** the invoice amount against stock value. If the net amount plus item tax and landed cost differs from the stock-ledger value, the difference is posted to the account returned by `get_stock_variance_account` (lines 523–533). - **Subcontracting:** a credit to the supplier-warehouse account for `rm_supp_cost`, if any. - **Landed cost:** credits to the landed cost voucher accounts, if any. - **Inventory account:** its debit comes from the Stock Ledger Entry, which the stock-posting code produces. For a Standard Cost item (valuation method "Standard Cost"), `get_stock_variance_account` returns the Purchase Price Variance account from `get_purchase_price_variance_account` in `item_standard_cost.py`. Other items get the company's `default_expense_account` instead. The variance is the gap between the invoice rate and the standard rate. **Where PPV is booked** - With Update Stock off, the PPV was booked earlier, on the Purchase Receipt. `get_divisional_loss_account` in `erpnext/stock/doctype/purchase_receipt/services/gl_composer.py` (lines 370–392) sends the receipt-rate vs standard-rate difference to the PPV account for Standard Cost items. - With Update Stock on, the invoice itself books the stock movement and the PPV.

final answer
**Update Stock off (invoice against a Standard Cost item's Purchase Receipt)** The invoice posts no Purchase Price Variance (PPV) and no stock-adjustment entry. The code is in `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries`, in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`. - The `update_stock and auto_accounting_for_stock` branch is skipped. So `make_stock_adjustment_entry` and `get_stock_variance_account` are never called. - The item falls into the `else` branch, which posts one debit for the full billed amount: - **Debit:** `item.expense_account`, or the deferred expense account if deferred expense applies. For a stock item bought through a Purchase Receipt, this is normally Stock Received But Not Billed (SRBNB). - **Amount:** `base_net_amount` (`base_amount` from `tax_service.get_amount_and_base_amount`). - **Against:** the supplier. - **Credit:** the supplier (payable) is posted by `make_supplier_gl_entry`. - A code comment says the linked Purchase Receipt already booked the stock at standard cost and the PPV. The invoice only clears SRBNB at the full billed amount. Booking PPV again would double count it and leave SRBNB partly uncleared. - If the exchange rate differs from the receipt's, the same branch can add a debit to the expense account and a credit to the exchange gain/loss account. This applies when `set_landed_cost_based_on_purchase_invoice_rate` is off, the item has a linked Purchase Receipt, and the net rate is unchanged. **Update Stock on (with perpetual inventory)** - The invoice creates its own Stock Ledger Entries (SLEs) and books the stock itself. - `make_stock_adjustment_entry` runs for each stock item (or fixed asset). - It debits `item.expense_account` with `warehouse_debit_amount`, which is `valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor`. If the SLE value differs, it uses the SLE's `stock_value_difference` instead. - If the invoice's valuation amount differs from the SLE value, it posts an extra "Stock Adjustment" debit. The difference is `warehouse_debit_amount − stock_amount`. The account comes from `get_stock_variance_account`. - For a Standard Cost item, that account is the Purchase Price Variance account, from `get_purchase_price_variance_account`. - For other items, it is the company's `default_expense_account`. - The same branch can add other entries: - the warehouse entries when `from_warehouse` is set; - landed-cost credits; - a subcontracting raw-material credit. - The stock-in-hand posting itself comes from the stock ledger posting. - For a return with Update Stock on, the variance is `stock_amount − warehouse_debit_amount`. It is also posted to the PPV account for Standard Cost items. **Difference:** with Update Stock off, the invoice posts only the single SRBNB-clearing debit, and the PPV was already booked on the Purchase Receipt. With Update Stock on, the invoice also books the stock and any standard-cost variance against the PPV account.

The code is in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/purchase_invoice/services/gl_composer.py`, in `PurchaseInvoiceGLComposer.make_item_gl_entries`. I read the code but did not run an invoice to confirm the entries. **Update Stock off** - The item goes to the `else` branch of `make_item_gl_entries`. The condition for the stock branch needs `doc.update_stock`, so it is skipped. - That branch posts one debit to `item.expense_account` for the full billed amount, with the supplier as the "against" account. The credit to the supplier is posted separately by `make_supplier_gl_entry`. - `ExpenseAccountService.set_expense_account` (in `services/expense_account.py`) sets `item.expense_account` to Stock Received But Not Billed (SRBNB). That happens when perpetual inventory is on, the item is a stock item, and a Purchase Receipt GL entry already booked SRBNB. So the debit clears SRBNB. - Because `make_stock_adjustment_entry` is not called, no PPV or stock-adjustment entry is posted. Posting PPV again would double count it and leave SRBNB partly uncleared. - If the exchange rate differs from the receipt's, the code also posts a debit to the expense account and an equal credit to the exchange gain/loss account. **Update Stock on** - The invoice itself moves stock and books its own stock entries. `make_stock_adjustment_entry` first sets `warehouse_debit_amount` to `valuation_rate × qty × conversion_factor`. final answer
**The pattern** ERPNext picks the "latest" row by turning a partial sort key into a total order. The date or datetime column stays the primary sort key, `DESC`. Then come unique columns as tiebreakers, usually `creation` and then `name`, both also `DESC`. A query that sorts on the date alone is only a partial order. When rows tie on the date, SQL leaves the choice among them undefined, and in practice it depends on the engine and its query plan. This is written down in two places: - `.github/POSTGRES_COMPATIBILITY.md` has an item called "`ORDER BY … LIMIT 1` with no unique tiebreaker". It says to add a `creation` or `name` tiebreaker **only if it doesn't change MariaDB's current pick**. A later section says to leave ties alone when the engines already agree, or when a tiebreaker would change MariaDB's result. - `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` is a pre-commit guard for MySQL-only SQL. Its docstring says it does not try to catch "ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 tiebreakers". Those need the test suite or a reviewer, so the pattern is enforced by review and tests rather than by a linter. **Why it matters across engines** MariaDB and PostgreSQL can pick different rows from a tie. The cause is differences in index and scan order, NULL ordering, and collation. The same data could then give different incoming rates, addresses or allocations depending on the database. Adding unique tiebreakers makes the pick identical on both. **Where it is applied** - **`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`, `get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos`**: orders by `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc` with `.limit(1)`. This is the clearest example. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py` covers it. Its docstring says `posting_date` alone is non-total, so two same-date SLEs with different `incoming_rate` could resolve differently. - **`erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py`**: the latest-SLE lookup uses `order_by="posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc", limit=1`. **The pattern** Ordering by a date alone doesn't give a total order. If two rows share that date, `ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 1` may return either one. ERPNext fixes this by appending tie-breaker columns to the sort until the order is total: - The usual form is `<date> desc, creation desc`, and sometimes `, name desc` is added. `creation` is the row's insert timestamp. `name` is unique, so it always settles the tie. - Where the sort key is a preference score, such as an address-type CASE expression, the code appends a unique column like `name` or `link.parent` ascending. **Why it matters across engines** When rows tie, SQL leaves the order undefined. MariaDB/InnoDB tends to return ties in index or primary-key order. Postgres can return them in whatever order the plan produces. The same data could therefore give different "latest" rows on the two engines, which gives different rates and different test results. Adding the unique tie-breaker makes the winner identical on both. The code comments say this directly: "total order so the latest SLE is picked identically on both engines" and "deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines". **Where it is applied** I found these by search and did not check every query in the repo. - `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py` - `update_entries_after.get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos` orders with `.orderby(posting_date desc).orderby(creation desc).orderby(name desc).limit(1)`. It picks the latest incoming rate for a serial number that was transferred to another company. - A query near line 1959 uses `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc`. - `erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py` - `set_stock_balance_as_per_serial_no` uses `order_by="posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc"` with `limit=1`. The comment says it was previously `posting_date` only. - Line 82 uses `posting_datetime desc, creation desc`. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py` - `get_item_standard_rate` orders by `effective_date desc, creation desc` with `limit=1`. Line 265 uses the same ordering. - `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_closing_entry/stock_closing_entry.py` (line 345) orders by `to_date desc, creation desc`. - `erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py` - `get_payer_address_html` and `get_street_address_html` sort by Postal and then Billing preference. They then add `.orderby(address.name)` or `.orderby(link.parent)` before `.limit(1)`. - Tests that lock the behaviour in: - `test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic` in `stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py`. It creates two same-date entries, `MAT-SLE-TIE-A` and `MAT-SLE-TIE-B`, and expects the later name to win. - `test_irs_1099.py`, which covers the address tie-break. - `test_stock_reconciliation.py`, `test_stock_entry.py` and `test_stock_balance.py`, which use `... desc, creation desc`. **Related cases** These are not date-based `LIMIT 1` picks, but they follow the same idea of making results the same on both engines: - `rfq_transaction_list` in `controllers/website_list_for_contact.py` selects `creation` because Postgres requires `SELECT DISTINCT` order-by columns to be in the select list. - `unreconcile_payment.py` adds an explicit order because Postgres `GROUP BY` doesn't imply ordering. - `sales_payment_summary.py` wraps non-grouped columns in `Max()`. Not every query is covered. `validate_for_closed_fiscal_year` in `repost_accounting_ledger.py` orders by `period_end_date desc` and `posting_date desc` alone. It only reads the date value, so a tie doesn't change its result.

**The pattern.** ERPNext adds extra, lower-priority sort keys after the date key. The usual chain is `date DESC, creation DESC, name DESC`. `name` is the primary key, so it is unique and the final key always breaks the tie. The queries are written with `frappe.qb` as chained `.orderby(..., order=frappe.qb.desc)` calls followed by `.limit(1)`. A few use `order_by="posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc"` strings or raw SQL. **Why it matters across engines.** SQL does not define which row comes first among rows that tie on the `ORDER BY` key. MariaDB/MySQL usually returns them in index or insertion order. PostgreSQL can return them in a different order, depending on the plan, sort algorithm or heap order. With `LIMIT 1` on a date-only sort, the same data can return different rows on different engines, or on different runs. A unique final key removes that ambiguity. The repo says this explicitly in comments: - `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` is a pre-commit guard. Its docstring lists "ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 tiebreakers" as a semantic divergence that static analysis cannot catch. Those cases need the test suite on a Postgres site or a human reviewer. - Code comments in the changed files say things like "deterministic LIMIT-1 tie-break across engines". - `serial_and_batch_bundle.py` has a related comment: Postgres requires `ORDER BY` columns to appear in the select list or the `GROUP BY`. **Where it is applied** (I confirmed these by grep and by reading the cited lines in three of them): - **`erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py`** uses `order_by="posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc"` (around line 322) and `"posting_datetime desc, creation desc"` (around line 82). - **`erpnext/assets/doctype/asset_movement/asset_movement.py`**: `get_latest_location_and_custodian` orders by `transaction_date DESC, name DESC` with `.limit(1)`. - MariaDB/InnoDB usually returns them in index or primary-key order, so it looks stable. Postgres makes no such promise, and `LIMIT 1` can return a different row from run to run. final answer
**The pattern.** ERPNext never relies on the date column alone. It appends further sort keys to every `ORDER BY <date> DESC … LIMIT 1` until the ordering is total. The usual order is date, then `creation DESC`, then `name DESC` (or `name` ascending for non-date picks). `name` is the primary key, so it is unique and gives a final tie-break. **Why it matters across engines.** With `ORDER BY posting_date DESC LIMIT 1`, rows that share the date are tied. SQL leaves their order undefined. MariaDB tends to return them in index or insertion order. Postgres can pick a different row, depending on the plan and heap order. The "latest" row, and any value taken from it such as a rate, can then differ between engines or between runs. Adding `creation` and `name` makes the same row win everywhere. Postgres adds a second constraint. With `SELECT DISTINCT`, every `ORDER BY` column must also be in the select list. `rfq_transaction_list` therefore selects `party.creation` explicitly, and `serial_and_batch_bundle.py` (around line 3426) has a comment saying the same. The repo's static checker `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` states that it does not catch these "ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 tiebreakers". They are left to the test suite or a reviewer, so each fix has a regression test. **Where it is applied:** - **`erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`, `update_entries_after.get_incoming_value_for_serial_nos`:** - It looks up the latest Stock Ledger Entry for a serial number that was transferred to another company. - It uses `orderby(posting_date desc).orderby(creation desc).orderby(name desc).limit(1)`. - `test_incoming_value_for_transferred_serial_no_is_deterministic` in `stock_ledger_entry/test_stock_ledger_entry.py` creates two same-date entries and asserts the later name wins, with a rate of 200. - **`stock_ledger.py` around line 1959:** a raw query using `order by posting_datetime desc, creation desc`. - **`erpnext/stock/stock_balance.py`:** - Line 82 uses `posting_datetime desc, creation desc`. - Line 322 uses `posting_date desc, creation desc, name desc`. - **`erpnext/stock/doctype/item_standard_cost/item_standard_cost.py`:** `get_item_standard_rate` and the query near line 265 use `effective_date desc, creation desc` with `limit=1`. - **`erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_closing_entry/stock_closing_entry.py`, `StockClosing.get_last_stock_closing_entry`:** uses `to_date desc, creation desc`. - **`erpnext/regional/report/irs_1099/irs_1099.py`, `get_payer_address_html` and `get_street_address_html`:** these order by CASE preference first, then `address.name` or `link.parent` as the tie-break before `limit(1)`. `test_irs_1099.py` covers it. - **Other tie-breaks outside the date-DESC case:** - `stock/get_item_details.py` (around line 1265, a final unique tie-break). - `payment_entry.py` (around line 2799, a unique tie-break for same-`transaction_date` rows). - `customer_acquisition_and_loyalty.py` (around line 169, a name tie-break). - `stock/doctype/packed_item/packed_item.py` (around line 329, a name tie-break). - `selling/page/point_of_sale/point_of_sale.py` (around line 467, a tie-break among contacts). **Not yet fixed.** `RepostAccountingLedger.validate_for_closed_fiscal_year` in `repost_accounting_ledger.py` orders by the date alone with `limit=1`. It only plucks that date, so the tie is harmless there.

final answer
On PostgreSQL, ERPNext uses three Postgres advisory locks, all keyed by item and warehouse. They sit on top of the normal `FOR UPDATE` row locks and a retry path for recoverable errors. I read the code but didn't run it or the tests. **1. Repost-vs-repost gate: `repost_gate(item_code, warehouse)` in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`** - `repost_future_sle` loops over `items_to_be_repost`. Each iteration wraps `update_entries_after(...)` in `with repost_gate(item_code, warehouse):`. - On Postgres, `repost_gate` returns `frappe.db.advisory_lock(("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)`. This is a session-level lock, and `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT` is 300 seconds. - Two background Repost Item Valuation jobs on the same pair therefore take turns. They no longer race into a lock-order deadlock between the inner `... for update` reads. - The row locks still enforce correctness. The gate only reduces deadlock and retry churn. - The key is a tuple, so a colon in an item code or warehouse name can't make two different pairs share a lock. - On MariaDB, or on a frappe version without `advisory_lock` (checked with `hasattr`), it returns `nullcontext()`. It then falls back to the plain deadlock-retry path. - The synchronous `repost_current_voucher` submit path is deliberately not gated. The code comment says blocking a submit behind a background repost would be worse. **2. Per-write gate: `sle_processing_gate(item_code, warehouse)` in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`** - This calls `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)`. It is transaction-scoped and re-entrant, and it is released at commit or rollback. - It is called from `make_sl_entries`, and from line 613 in the same file, which I didn't open. - In `make_sl_entries` the pairs are sorted first (`sorted({(item_code, warehouse)...})`). Two vouchers touching the same pairs therefore always take the locks in the same order, which avoids deadlock. - The reason for the gate is that MariaDB's gap locks make concurrent inserts visible to the previous-SLE locking reads. Postgres locking reads can't see rows another transaction is inserting. Without the gate, two writers would compute from the same stale previous SLE, and one Bin write would be lost. **3. Batch average-rate gate: `BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate` in `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`** - For outward entries (`actual_qty <= 0`) on Postgres, it first calls `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("batch-valuation", item_code, warehouse))`. - Only then does it run `get_batch_stock_before_date()`, which sums `stock_value_difference` and `qty` per batch, and compute `batch_avg_rate`. - That query's `FOR UPDATE` is skipped on Postgres (`if frappe.db.db_type != "postgres"`). Postgres rejects `FOR UPDATE` together with `GROUP BY`, and row-locking the whole history would write a lock marker on every tuple. MariaDB keeps the grouped `FOR UPDATE` plus gap locks. - The result is that two concurrent outward valuations of the same item-warehouse's batches are serialized, so neither computes the average from a stale history. - Inward entries just read `total_amount` from the bundle, so they need no lock. - `erpnext/stock/deprecated_serial_batch.py` carries comments saying the same lock covers the legacy valuation path. **Recovery: `erpnext/stock/doctype/repost_item_valuation/repost_item_valuation.py`** - `RecoverableErrors = (JobTimeoutException, QueryDeadlockError, QueryTimeoutError)`. If a deadlock still happens, or a gate wait times out, the job is re-queued and stays "In Progress" instead of being marked Failed. That is why the 300-second timeout is kept well under the 1800-second repost job limit. - `test_repost_item_valuation.py` has a test that a `QueryDeadlockError` leaves the status as "In Progress". The pg_locks-based tests are in `test_stock_ledger_entry.py` and `test_serial_and_batch_bundle.py`.

PostgreSQL has no gap locks, and its locking reads can't see rows another transaction is inserting. On PostgreSQL, ERPNext uses three advisory locks to keep concurrent stock jobs from deadlocking or double-computing the average rate. They are keyed on the item-warehouse pair, and `FOR UPDATE` row locks still enforce correctness underneath them. I read the code but did not run it against PostgreSQL. 1. **Repost gate (`repost_gate` in `erpnext/stock/stock_ledger.py`)** - `repost_future_sle` wraps each `update_entries_after(...)` call in `with repost_gate(item_code, warehouse):`. - On PostgreSQL, `repost_gate` takes a session-level `frappe.db.advisory_lock(("stock_repost", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)`. - The lock is taken before the inner `... for update` row locks. Two background reposts of the same pair therefore take turns instead of racing into a lock-order deadlock. - The key is a tuple, so a colon in an item code or warehouse name can't make two different pairs collide on one lock. - It guards repost against repost only. The synchronous `repost_current_voucher` path on submit is deliberately not gated, so a submit never blocks behind a background repost. That path relies on the existing deadlock retry. - It is skipped on MariaDB and on a frappe version without `advisory_lock` (`hasattr` check). In both cases it returns `nullcontext()`. - `REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT` is 300 seconds, well under the 1800-second repost job timeout. A waiter that times out raises a recoverable `QueryTimeoutError`, re-queues, and frees its worker slot. 2. **Stock ledger entry gate (`sle_processing_gate` in the same file)** - It takes a transaction-scoped `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("stock-sle", item_code, warehouse), timeout=REPOST_LOCK_TIMEOUT)`. - It is re-entrant and released at commit or rollback, so stock submissions for one item-warehouse pair don't lose writes. Without it, PostgreSQL would fall back to serialization-failure retries. 3. **Batch valuation lock (`BatchNoValuation.calculate_avg_rate` in `erpnext/stock/serial_batch_bundle.py`)** - For outward entries (`actual_qty <= 0`) on PostgreSQL, it first calls `frappe.db.transaction_advisory_lock(("batch-valuation", sle.item_code, sle.warehouse))`. - Only then does it call `get_batch_stock_before_date()` and compute the average rate and stock value difference. Concurrent jobs therefore can't both compute the average rate from the same history. - MariaDB gets the same serialization from its grouped `FOR UPDATE` and gap locks on those history reads. PostgreSQL has no gap locks, and row-locking the whole history would write a lock marker on every tuple. Any other exception sets "Failed". - This is matched by exception type, because the old traceback string-match only recognised MariaDB's "Deadlock found" and missed PostgreSQL's "deadlock detected".

final answer
Two workers can't pick up the same date/report-type row, for three reasons. Each row is claimed under a row lock that skips locked rows. The claim is recorded as a status change that is committed before any worker runs. And a worker only runs a row whose status is `Running`. All of this is in `erpnext/accounts/doctype/process_period_closing_voucher/process_period_closing_voucher.py`. The unit of work is a row in the child table `Process Period Closing Voucher Detail`. Each row has a `processing_date`, a `report_type`, a `parentfield` and a `status`. The status moves from `Queued` to `Running` to `Completed`. 1. **Claiming a row.** Both `initialize_parallel_threads(docname)` and `schedule_next_date(docname)` select rows with `status = "Queued"` for that parent. They order them by `parentfield, idx, processing_date`, and the query ends in `.for_update(skip_locked=True)`. That is `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. If another transaction has already locked a row, the query skips it and takes the next one. `initialize_parallel_threads` claims up to 4 rows. `schedule_next_date` claims 1. 2. **Marking it as taken.** Straight after the select, the code sets each claimed row to `status = "Running"`. When a Stock Entry is made from a Job Card, the system pre-fills serial numbers or batches by looking at what earlier operations of the same Work Order produced and left in the source warehouse. If fewer units are available than the row's quantity, it fills what exists and leaves the shortfall blank. I read the code but did not run it. **Where it starts** - `make_stock_entry` in `erpnext/manufacturing/doctype/job_card/mapper.py` builds a "Material Transfer for Manufacture" Stock Entry from the Job Card. - Its `set_missing_values` step loops over every item row and calls `set_previous_operation_serial_batch(target, item)`. - That function is in `erpnext/stock/doctype/stock_entry/services/manufacturing.py`. The Manufacture stock entry type also calls it from `ManufactureEntry.add_raw_materials`. **When it applies** `set_previous_operation_serial_batch` does nothing in any of these cases: - The Stock Entry has no `work_order`. - The row has no `s_warehouse`. - The row quantity, converted by the row's `conversion_factor`, is zero or less. - The row already has a serial and batch bundle, a `serial_no` or a `batch_no`. **How the candidates are chosen** `get_previous_operation_output_sn_batch(work_order, item_code, s_warehouse)` builds the pool of serials and batches: 1. The item must be the `finished_good` of some Work Order Operation on that Work Order. Ordinary raw materials return an empty pool. 2. The item must have `has_serial_no` or `has_batch_no`, otherwise the pool is empty. 3. Produced stock comes from submitted "Manufacture" Stock Entries of the same Work Order. It counts only finished-item rows (`is_finished_item=1`) whose target warehouse is the row's source warehouse. 4. Consumed stock comes from submitted Stock Entries of the same Work Order with the same item whose source warehouse is that warehouse. 5. Both sets are read from the Serial and Batch Entry rows of each entry's bundle, ignoring cancelled rows. This is done in `_get_operation_bundles` and `_get_operation_sn_batch`. 6. The pool is produced minus consumed. For serials, it keeps those not already consumed. For batches, it keeps `produced qty − consumed qty` where that is above zero. **What happens when fewer units are available than the row's quantity** - `_cap_pool_to_qty` trims the pool to the row quantity. For serials it takes the first `int(qty)` in the order they were produced. For batches it goes through them in order, taking `min(batch_qty, remaining)` until the quantity is met. - If the pool is smaller than the quantity, it simply takes everything available and does not raise an error. The docstring says it "fill[s] what is available and leav[es] any shortfall blank for the user". - If the pool is empty, the function returns and the row is left untouched. - Otherwise it creates a draft Serial and Batch Bundle with `SerialBatchCreation(...).make_serial_and_batch_bundle()`. The bundle is outward, `do_not_submit=True`, with `qty` set to the full row quantity, and it carries only the serials or batches that were found. - The row then gets `serial_and_batch_bundle = bundle.name` and `use_serial_batch_fields = 0`. The user has to add the missing serials or batches before submitting.

**Mechanism.** ERPNext uses database savepoints through Frappe's `frappe.db.savepoint(name)` and `frappe.db.rollback(save_point=name)`. The pattern is: 1. Call `frappe.db.savepoint("x")` just before the risky write. 2. Run the write in a `try` block. 3. In the `except` block, call `frappe.db.rollback(save_point="x")`. On PostgreSQL, a failed statement aborts the whole transaction until you roll back. Rolling back to the savepoint clears that aborted state, so later statements can run. **How it differs from a full rollback.** - A plain `frappe.db.rollback()` discards the entire transaction. That includes the parent document and any earlier work. - A savepoint rollback undoes only the writes made since the savepoint. The outer transaction stays open and its earlier changes are kept. - Several call sites say this in comments. Examples are `# preserve transaction in postgres`, and the `frappe_crm_api.py` comment that a failure "does NOT discard the Customer". **Where it is applied.** I found these by grepping for `savepoint`. ERPNext handles this with database savepoints. The pattern is `frappe.db.savepoint(name)` before the risky write, then `frappe.db.rollback(save_point=name)` in the `except` block. I found it by grepping for `savepoint` under `erpnext/` and read three of the call sites. I did not open the others, so their descriptions below come from grep hits and comments only. **How it works** On PostgreSQL, one failed statement, such as a unique-key violation, aborts the whole transaction. Every later statement then fails with "current transaction is aborted". A savepoint marks a point inside the open transaction. Rolling back to it undoes only the writes made since the mark, which also clears the aborted state. **How it differs from a full rollback** - A plain `frappe.db.rollback()` discards the entire transaction. That would throw away the parent document being submitted, earlier loop iterations and any queued work. - `rollback(save_point=...)` discards only the failed part. The outer transaction stays open and can still commit. - The code comments say this directly: "preserve transaction in postgres", "a failure here does NOT discard the Customer just…", and "Rolling back to a savepoint keeps both." **Where it is applied** - `erpnext/stock/utils.py`, `_create_bin`: it sets a `create_bin` savepoint and inserts a Bin. On `frappe.UniqueValidationError` (a concurrent insert) it rolls back to the savepoint and fetches the existing Bin with `get_last_doc`. - `erpnext/accounts/doctype/payment_entry/payment_entry.py`, `trigger_invoice_update_for_subscriptions`: this is the clearest best-effort case. It uses a `subscription_update` savepoint around `refresh_subscription_status()`. On any exception it rolls back to the savepoint and calls `frappe.log_error`, so the Payment Entry submit carries on. - `erpnext/accounts/doctype/fiscal_year/fiscal_year.py`, the auto-create fiscal year scheduler job: it uses `auto_create_fiscal_year`, so a duplicate-year INSERT does not poison the scheduler transaction. - `erpnext/crm/frappe_crm_api.py`: it uses `crm_create_address` and `crm_customer_links`. A failure while linking contacts or addresses does not discard the Customer that was just created. - `erpnext/erpnext_integrations/doctype/plaid_settings/plaid_settings.py`: it uses `plaid_bank_account`, `plaid_update_account` and a per-transaction `plaid_sync_txn`. - `erpnext/accounts/doctype/opening_invoice_creation_tool/opening_invoice_creation_tool.py`: it uses a unique savepoint name per invoice, built from `frappe.generate_hash`, and calls `rollback(save_point=savepoint)` so a failure only undoes that invoice. - `erpnext/stock/report/stock_and_account_value_comparison/stock_and_account_value_comparison.py`: it uses `repost_based_on_transaction` so an already-queued repost (`DuplicateEntryError`) does not affect the others. - Other uses, from grep only: - `erpnext/utilities/bulk_transaction.py` - `erpnext/accounts/bulk_payment.py` - `erpnext/accounts/doctype/ledger_merge/ledger_merge.py` - `erpnext/assets/doctype/asset/depreciation.py` - `erpnext/subcontracting/doctype/subcontracting_receipt/mapper.py` - `erpnext/buying/doctype/purchase_order/mapper.py` - `erpnext/telephony/doctype/call_log/call_log.py` - `erpnext/crm/doctype/email_campaign/email_campaign.py` - `erpnext/accounts/doctype/bank_transaction/bank_transaction_upload.py` - `erpnext/stock/reorder_item.py` - `erpnext/regional/doctype/import_supplier_invoice/import_supplier_invoice.py` - `erpnext/setup/setup_wizard/operations/install_fixtures.py` - `erpnext/setup/setup_wizard/operations/taxes_setup.py` - `erpnext/setup/demo.py` - `erpnext/patches/v13_0/trim_whitespace_from_serial_nos.py` - `erpnext/controllers/ledger_preview.py` uses a `ledger_preview` savepoint for a different purpose. It submits the document in memory to read the GL and stock ledger entries, then rolls back to the savepoint so the preview never persists anything. `.github/helper/postgres_compat.py` mentions "savepoint discipline" as something its automated check cannot catch, so it is left to tests and reviewers.

It also clears any queued after-commit hooks. - `rollback(save_point=...)` runs `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`. It undoes only the writes made since the savepoint. The outer transaction stays open and keeps its earlier work. - On PostgreSQL, a failed statement puts the transaction in an aborted state, and every later statement fails until it is rolled back. Rolling back to the savepoint clears that state, so the code can carry on. - MariaDB doesn't abort the transaction on a failed statement, so the savepoint matters mostly on PostgreSQL. **Where it is applied** Optional or auto-created documents: - `erpnext/accounts/doctype/fiscal_year/fiscal_year.py` uses the savepoint `auto_create_fiscal_year`.
